questions.question: What is the difference between Spring Framework and Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Framework vs Spring Boot — What's the Difference?
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot is not a replacement for Spring Framework — it's an opinionated layer on top that eliminates boilerplate configuration. Spring provides the ecosystem (IoC, AOP, MVC, Data, Security), while Spring Boot provides auto-configuration, embedded servers, starter dependencies, and production-ready defaults so you can go from zero to running application in minutes instead of hours.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that Spring Boot builds on top of Spring Framework rather than replacing it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'Spring Boot is a different framework' or treating them as competitors rather than layers in the same stack.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that understanding raw Spring is still essential for debugging auto-configuration issues, and mention the --debug flag for the conditions evaluation report.

sections.title: Boot Is Not a Separate Framework — It's the Configuration You'd Write Yourself
sections.content:
The most common way candidates fail this question is by framing Spring Boot as a competitor to Spring Framework. In reality, **every Spring Boot application is a Spring Framework application** — Boot is an opinionated configuration layer that sits on top of the same IoC container, the same AOP proxy infrastructure, and the same MVC dispatcher you'd wire manually.

What Boot actually replaces is ceremony, not capability. In a raw Spring project, you write `@Configuration` classes to define your `DataSource`, register your `ViewResolver`, configure your `DispatcherServlet`, and manually align dozens of transitive dependency versions. A single version mismatch between Hibernate and Spring Data JPA can cost you a full day of debugging `NoSuchMethodError` stack traces that reveal nothing about the actual problem.

**Spring Boot eliminates that configuration tax** through three mechanisms: auto-configuration classes that detect what's on your classpath and apply sensible defaults, starter POMs that bundle pre-tested dependency versions, and an embedded server that turns deployment from a multi-step WAR packaging process into `java -jar app.jar`. The framework underneath hasn't changed — you've just stopped writing the boilerplate that connects it.

sections.title: What Boot Automates vs What Spring Framework Still Controls
sections.content:
The table below isn't a feature list — it maps each pain point in raw Spring to the specific Boot mechanism that eliminates it.

| Concern | Spring Framework (Manual) | Spring Boot (Auto-Configured) |
|---|---|---|
| **Bean configuration** | Write `@Configuration` classes for every integration | `@ConditionalOnClass` auto-detects and wires beans |
| **Server deployment** | Package as WAR, deploy to external Tomcat or JBoss | Embedded Tomcat starts from `main()` — one JAR, no server install |
| **Dependency versions** | Manually align 30+ transitive JARs | Starter POMs with a tested version matrix managed by the Spring team |
| **DataSource setup** | Define `HikariDataSource` bean with explicit URL and pool config | Add `spring.datasource.url` to `application.yml` — HikariCP auto-configured |
| **Production monitoring** | Build custom health checks and metrics endpoints from scratch | Actuator exposes `/health`, `/metrics`, `/info` out of the box |
| **Property management** | `PropertyPlaceholderConfigurer` with manual file loading | `application.yml` loaded automatically with profile support built in |

Notice the pattern: **the right column is what Boot does for you, the middle column is what you debug when it does the wrong thing.** That middle column is why understanding raw Spring still matters — every auto-configuration decision Boot makes maps directly to a manual configuration step you'd take yourself.

sections.title: When Auto-Configuration Does Something Unexpected — The --debug Flag That Most Developers Don't Know
sections.content:
Every Spring Boot auto-configuration class is guarded by `@Conditional` annotations — `@ConditionalOnClass` checks if a class exists on the classpath, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` backs off when you define your own bean, and `@ConditionalOnProperty` checks for specific property values. This conditional mechanism is what makes Boot feel like magic, and it's exactly what you need to understand when that magic breaks.

The most common production surprise is a bean you expected to be auto-configured that isn't — or one you didn't expect that is. When this happens, **run your application with the `--debug` flag** (or set `debug=true` in `application.properties`). Spring Boot prints a conditions evaluation report showing every auto-configuration class that was matched or excluded, with the exact condition that decided it.

```
=== CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT ===
Positive matches:
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found 'javax.sql.DataSource'

Negative matches:
   ActiveMQAutoConfiguration:
      Did not match:
         - @ConditionalOnClass did not find 'javax.jms.ConnectionFactory'
```

This report tells you exactly which decisions Boot made and why. When a `DataSource` isn't being created despite having the right dependency, the report will show which `@Conditional` check failed. **Being able to explain this debugging workflow** in an interview is what separates a developer who uses Boot from one who understands it. The right mental model isn't "Spring Boot is simpler" — it's "Spring Boot automates the decisions I'd make manually, and I know how to audit those decisions when they go wrong."

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Boot is not a replacement — it is Spring Framework with conventions applied** — auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter POMs eliminate XML setup; the underlying IoC container, AOP, and data layers are unchanged.
- **Auto-configuration is always conditional** — every auto-config class uses `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`; override any default by providing your own bean.
- **`@SpringBootApplication` = `@Configuration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan`** — knowing which composed annotation provides which behavior is a common interview checkpoint.
- **Raw Spring knowledge is still required for debugging** — when auto-configuration activates the wrong bean, understanding `BeanPostProcessor`, `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`, and condition evaluation is the only path to the root cause.
- **Spring Boot 3.x requires Java 17+ and Jakarta EE 9+ namespace** — `javax.*` is replaced by `jakarta.*`; a common migration trap for teams upgrading from Boot 2.x.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot is not a different framework — it is Spring Framework with decisions already made for you. The same `ApplicationContext`, the same IoC container, the same AOP proxies. What Spring Boot adds is conventions, auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter POMs that wire everything together automatically.

**What Spring Boot adds**
- Auto-configuration: Spring Boot reads `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` conditions at startup and registers beans only when the right dependencies are on the classpath and you have not already defined your own
- Embedded server: Tomcat, Jetty, or Netty ships inside the JAR — no deployment to an external container required
- Starter POMs: `spring-boot-starter-web` pulls in exactly the right set of dependencies at compatible versions

**What stays the same**
- The IoC container is identical — `ApplicationContext`, `BeanPostProcessor`, `@Autowired`, `@Transactional` all work exactly as in raw Spring
- Debugging an auto-configuration issue requires understanding raw Spring: which `BeanPostProcessor` runs, what condition failed, why two beans of the same type conflict

**When to use raw Spring**
- Embedding Spring into a non-boot environment (legacy app servers, custom tooling)
- Writing a Spring Boot starter or auto-configuration itself

`@SpringBootApplication` is three annotations composed: `@Configuration` (this class defines beans), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (activate auto-config), `@ComponentScan` (scan this package). Understanding the composition means you can decompose it when you only need part of it.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work internally?
questions.title: Spring Boot Auto-Configuration — How It Works Internally
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configuration uses @EnableAutoConfiguration to scan META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (or spring.factories in older versions) for candidate configuration classes. Each candidate is conditionally applied using @ConditionalOn* annotations that check for the presence of classes, beans, or properties. This lets Spring Boot configure sensible defaults without requiring explicit XML or Java configuration from the developer.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the mechanism behind Spring Boot's 'magic' rather than just using it as a black box.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Candidates often say 'Spring Boot just auto-configures things' without explaining how conditions and imports files drive the process.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the difference between spring.factories (pre-2.7) and AutoConfiguration.imports (2.7+), and how @AutoConfigureAfter/@AutoConfigureBefore control ordering.

sections.title: Auto-Configuration Isn't Magic — It's a Pipeline of Conditional @Configuration Classes
sections.content:
Most developers describe Spring Boot auto-configuration as "it just figures out what you need." That's the experience, not the mechanism. Under the hood, auto-configuration is a deterministic pipeline: Boot discovers a list of candidate `@Configuration` classes from a well-known file on the classpath, evaluates a set of `@Conditional` annotations on each one, and only registers the beans from classes whose conditions all pass.

**There is no scanning, no guessing, no AI.** Every auto-configuration class is a regular `@Configuration` class with `@Bean` methods — the same kind you'd write yourself. The only difference is that each one is guarded by conditions like `@ConditionalOnClass` ("only if this class is on the classpath"), `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` ("only if the developer hasn't already defined this bean"), and `@ConditionalOnProperty` ("only if this property is set"). When you add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` to your POM, Boot doesn't "detect" that you want JPA — it finds `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` in its imports file, checks that `javax.sql.DataSource` is on the classpath, confirms you haven't defined your own, and wires one with HikariCP defaults.

sections.title: Discovery — How Boot Finds 150+ Candidate Configuration Classes
sections.content:
When `@SpringBootApplication` triggers `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, Spring imports `AutoConfigurationImportSelector`, which reads a file that lists every auto-configuration class Boot ships. **In Spring Boot 2.7+**, this file is `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` — one fully-qualified class name per line. In older versions, the same list lived in `META-INF/spring.factories` under the `EnableAutoConfiguration` key.

The migration happened because `spring.factories` was overloaded — it handled auto-configuration, listeners, initializers, and failure analyzers all in one file. The new dedicated imports file is faster to parse and makes it obvious which classes are auto-configuration candidates.

Spring Boot 3.x ships roughly **150 auto-configuration classes** in this file. Every one of them is loaded as a candidate — but loading the class doesn't mean its beans get registered. That decision happens in the next phase. The key insight is that discovery is exhaustive and condition evaluation is selective. Boot loads all candidates and then filters, rather than trying to discover only the relevant ones.

sections.title: Condition Evaluation — The Chain of @ConditionalOn* Annotations That Decides Everything
sections.content:
Each auto-configuration class is decorated with one or more `@Conditional` annotations. Spring evaluates them in a specific order optimized for speed — cheap checks first, expensive checks last.

The most common conditions form a decision chain. `@ConditionalOnClass` checks whether a class exists on the classpath without actually loading it — this is the cheapest filter and eliminates most candidates immediately. If you don't have `javax.jms.ConnectionFactory` on your classpath, `ActiveMQAutoConfiguration` is skipped before any bean definitions are read.

Next, `@ConditionalOnProperty` checks application properties. A class guarded by `@ConditionalOnProperty(name = "spring.data.redis.repositories.enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)` will activate by default but can be disabled with a single property. This is how you turn off auto-configuration selectively without using `exclude`.

The most important condition for developers is **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`**. This is what makes Boot non-invasive — it checks whether a bean of a specific type already exists in the context. If you define your own `DataSource` bean, Boot's auto-configured one backs off silently. This is the mechanism behind "convention over configuration" — Boot provides the convention, your explicit bean is the configuration that overrides it.

When an auto-configuration doesn't behave as expected, run with `--debug` or set `debug=true` in `application.properties`. Boot prints a **conditions evaluation report** listing every candidate class and exactly which condition passed or failed. This report is the single most useful debugging tool for auto-configuration issues.

sections.title: Ordering and Exclusion — Why @AutoConfigureAfter Exists and How to Disable What You Don't Want
sections.content:
Auto-configuration classes don't run in random order — they declare dependencies on each other using `@AutoConfigureAfter` and `@AutoConfigureBefore`. For example, `JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration` declares `@AutoConfigureAfter(DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` because JPA repositories need a DataSource to already exist.

**Getting the ordering wrong in a custom auto-configuration is a common source of `BeanCreationException`** at startup. If your auto-configuration creates a bean that depends on another auto-configured bean, you must declare the ordering explicitly — Spring won't infer it from the bean dependency graph at the auto-configuration level.

To exclude an auto-configuration entirely, use `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` or set `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` in properties. The exclude approach is cleaner than fighting conditions with dummy beans.

The combination of discovery, conditions, and ordering produces a fully deterministic startup. Given the same classpath, the same properties, and the same user-defined beans, Boot will always produce the same application context. When something changes — a new JAR on the classpath, a removed property — you can trace exactly which condition flipped and which beans appeared or disappeared.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@EnableAutoConfiguration` loads candidate classes from `AutoConfiguration.imports`** — Spring Boot 2.7+ uses `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`; pre-2.7 used `META-INF/spring.factories`.
- **Every auto-config class is `@Conditional` — never truly unconditional** — `@ConditionalOnClass` checks the classpath; `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` checks the registry; user-defined beans always take precedence.
- **Auto-configuration runs after user configuration** — `@Configuration` classes from your packages are processed first; auto-config is effectively the fallback.
- **`--debug` prints the Conditions Evaluation Report** — three sections: positive (matched and applied), negative (checked and skipped), exclusions; the only reliable way to know why an auto-config fired or did not.
- **`spring.autoconfigure.exclude` removes a class entirely** — prevents an auto-config from being evaluated even if its conditions would match; useful when a starter pulls in something you do not want.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When Spring Boot 'just works' without any configuration, auto-configuration is what is happening behind the scenes. It is not magic — it is conditional bean registration driven by what is on your classpath and what beans you have already defined.

**How it is discovered**
- `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, which reads `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Spring Boot 2.7+) listing hundreds of candidate auto-configuration classes
- Each class is evaluated for its `@Conditional` annotations before any beans are created

**How conditions decide what registers**
- `@ConditionalOnClass(HikariDataSource.class)` — only apply this config if HikariCP is on the classpath
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` — only apply if you have not already defined a `DataSource`; this is how your custom bean overrides the default
- Your `@Configuration` classes are processed before auto-configuration — auto-config is always the fallback, never the override

**Debugging**
- Add `--debug` to the JVM arguments and Spring prints the Conditions Evaluation Report at startup
- Three sections: positive matches (auto-config that ran), negative matches (auto-config that was skipped and why), and exclusions
- `spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration` removes a class entirely when a starter pulls in something unwanted

questions.question: What are the key phases of the Spring Boot startup sequence when SpringApplication.run() is called?
questions.title: Spring Boot Startup Sequence (SpringApplication.run Phases)
questions.direct_answer: SpringApplication.run() orchestrates a multi-phase startup: it prepares the environment, creates and refreshes the ApplicationContext, then calls runners and publishes a final ready event. Each phase is observable via SpringApplicationRunListeners and ApplicationEvents. Understanding this sequence is critical for troubleshooting slow startups and for hooking in custom initialization logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can trace the lifecycle beyond 'the context starts' and explain where things like property loading and bean initialization happen.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner (called after context is ready) with @PostConstruct (called during bean initialization inside context refresh).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention SpringApplicationRunListeners and the exact ApplicationEvent types (ApplicationStartingEvent, ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent, etc.) and where to hook custom logic safely.

sections.title: Why Knowing the Startup Sequence Matters More Than Memorizing Event Names
sections.content:
Most developers think of `SpringApplication.run()` as "it starts the app." But this single method orchestrates a multi-phase lifecycle where **the order of operations determines where your custom logic can safely run.** The most common bug from misunderstanding this sequence is putting initialization code in `@PostConstruct` that depends on the full application context being ready — it isn't. `@PostConstruct` runs during bean initialization inside context refresh, before runners, before the server port is bound, and before `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires.

The startup sequence is observable through `SpringApplicationRunListeners`, which broadcast typed events at each phase boundary. These aren't just debugging aids — they're the hook points where you can inject custom behavior: registering metrics before the context exists, modifying the environment before property binding, or running migration scripts after the context is fully wired but before the app accepts traffic.

Understanding the sequence also explains why startup is slow. Each phase has a measurable cost, and Spring Boot 3.x added startup tracking via `ApplicationStartup` to let you pinpoint exactly which phase is consuming time.

sections.title: Environment and Context Creation — From System Properties to a Wired ApplicationContext
sections.content:
The first thing `SpringApplication.run()` does is create a `DefaultBootstrapContext` and notify `SpringApplicationRunListeners` with an `ApplicationStartingEvent`. At this point, **no beans exist, no properties are loaded, and no ApplicationContext has been created.** The only things running are listeners registered via `spring.factories` — this is where logging framework initialization happens.

Next comes environment preparation. Spring builds the `Environment` object by layering property sources in a specific precedence order: system properties override `application.yml`, which overrides `application.properties`, which overrides defaults. **`ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent`** fires here — it's the last safe point to programmatically add or modify property sources before anything reads them. If you need to inject secrets from a vault, this is where you do it.

With the environment ready, Spring creates the `ApplicationContext` — `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext` for web apps, `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` for non-web. The context type is inferred from the classpath (presence of `Servlet` API vs. reactive `WebFlux`). The context is created but **not yet refreshed** — no bean definitions have been processed.

sections.title: Context Refresh — Where Bean Instantiation, @PostConstruct, and Auto-Configuration All Happen
sections.content:
Context refresh is the heaviest phase and where most startup time is spent. `ApplicationPreparedEvent` fires just before refresh begins — the context exists, the main configuration class is registered, but no beans have been instantiated yet.

During refresh, Spring processes all `@Configuration` classes (including auto-configurations filtered by `@Conditional` annotations), creates bean definitions, and then instantiates singletons. **This is when `@PostConstruct` methods run** — during individual bean initialization, inside the refresh cycle. A common mistake is assuming `@PostConstruct` has access to the complete application context. It doesn't — other singletons may not have been created yet, and the web server hasn't started.

For web applications, context refresh also creates and starts the embedded server. The server binds to its port during refresh, which is why a port conflict causes `ApplicationContext` refresh failure, not a separate error. `ContextRefreshedEvent` fires when refresh completes — all singleton beans are instantiated, all `@PostConstruct` methods have run, and the server is listening.

The critical insight for interviews: **everything inside refresh happens before the application is considered "started."** If your initialization depends on all beans being ready, refresh is too early. You need the next phase.

sections.title: Runners and Ready — The Safe Zone for Application-Level Initialization
sections.content:
After context refresh completes, Boot fires `ApplicationStartedEvent` and calls all `CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner` beans. This is the first point where **every singleton bean is guaranteed to exist, every `@PostConstruct` has completed, and the server is bound to its port.** Runners are the correct place for one-time initialization tasks: loading caches, running data migrations, or verifying external service connectivity.

The difference between the two runner types is small but matters. `CommandLineRunner` receives raw `String[] args`, while `ApplicationRunner` receives an `ApplicationArguments` object that parses option arguments (like `--server.port=8081`) from non-option arguments. Use `@Order` to control runner execution sequence when you have multiple.

Finally, `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires — this is the signal that the application is fully initialized and ready to accept requests. Health check endpoints like `/actuator/health` should return UP only after this event. In Kubernetes, this maps to the **readiness probe** — your pod should not receive traffic until `ApplicationReadyEvent` has fired.

If any runner throws an exception, the startup fails and `ApplicationFailedEvent` fires instead of `ApplicationReadyEvent`. This is the clean distinction: `ApplicationStartedEvent` means "context is refreshed," `ApplicationReadyEvent` means "everything succeeded, accept traffic."

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PostConstruct` fires before runners; runners fire after the context is fully ready** — the order is: instantiate beans → inject → `@PostConstruct` → `ApplicationStartedEvent` → runners → `ApplicationReadyEvent`.
- **`CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner` execute after all beans are created** — safe to call any injected service; `@PostConstruct` is not safe for logic that depends on the full context being operational.
- **Multiple runners use `@Order` or `Ordered`** — lower value = higher priority; unordered runners execute in registration order.
- **`SpringApplicationRunListeners` vs `ApplicationListener`** — `SpringApplicationRunListeners` fire before the `ApplicationContext` is created (too early for `@Bean`); `ApplicationListener` or `@EventListener` fires after.
- **`ApplicationFailedEvent` fires if startup fails** — use it to emit metrics or alerts before the JVM exits; not fired on graceful shutdown, only on exception during startup.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot's startup follows a precise sequence that determines when each hook is safe to use. Getting the order wrong means initialization code runs before its dependencies are ready.

**The sequence**
- Spring creates and injects all beans, then calls `@PostConstruct` methods — dependencies are available but the web server has not started yet
- `ApplicationStartedEvent` fires after the context is refreshed and the embedded server is started
- `CommandLineRunner` and `ApplicationRunner` beans execute next — this is the last point before `ApplicationReadyEvent` marks the application as ready for traffic
- `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires when the application is fully started and health checks are passing

**What goes where**
- `@PostConstruct`: initialization that depends only on injected collaborators — cache warmup, connection validation
- Runners: startup logic that should run after the full context is ready — data seeding, integration checks, feature flag registration
- `@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)`: same timing as runners but declared as an event listener rather than implementing an interface

Multiple runners execute in `@Order` sequence — lower value runs first. `CommandLineRunner` receives raw `String[] args`; `ApplicationRunner` receives a typed `ApplicationArguments` object — the only practical difference between the two.

These aren't just debugging aids — they're the hook points where you can inject custom behavior: registering metrics before the context exists, modifying the environment before property binding.

questions.question: What does @SpringBootApplication do and what three annotations does it combine?
questions.title: @SpringBootApplication — What It Combines
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootApplication is a convenience meta-annotation that combines @SpringBootConfiguration (a specialised @Configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration (triggers auto-configuration scanning), and @ComponentScan (scans the package of the annotated class and its sub-packages for Spring components). Placing it on your main class is equivalent to annotating it with all three separately.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands component scanning scope and can explain why placing the main class in the root package matters.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing the main class inside a sub-package so that sibling packages are missed by @ComponentScan, causing beans not to be found.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that you can narrow or widen the scan with scanBasePackages/scanBasePackageClasses, and that @SpringBootConfiguration differs from @Configuration because only one is allowed per application context.

sections.title: Three Annotations in a Trenchcoat — And Why Package Placement Is the Hidden Gotcha
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` is a meta-annotation that combines three annotations into one. Knowing the three names is the easy part — understanding **what each one actually triggers and the subtle constraint that catches most teams** is what interviewers are really testing.

The three annotations are `@SpringBootConfiguration` (a specialized `@Configuration` that marks this class as the application's primary configuration source), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (triggers the auto-configuration pipeline that scans `AutoConfiguration.imports` for conditional configuration classes), and `@ComponentScan` (scans the package of the annotated class and all sub-packages for `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` beans).

The critical detail is `@ComponentScan`'s default behavior. It scans **from the package of the annotated class downward.** If your main class lives in `com.example.app.config` and your controllers are in `com.example.app.web`, both get scanned. But if your main class is in `com.example.app.config` and your service is in `com.example.service`, that service package is a sibling, not a child — **it will never be found.** This is the most common reason for "bean not found" errors in new Spring Boot projects.

sections.title: What Each Annotation Controls and How to Override the Defaults
sections.content:
**`@SpringBootConfiguration`** differs from plain `@Configuration` in one important way: Spring Boot enforces that only one `@SpringBootConfiguration` exists per application context. This prevents accidental duplicate context creation in tests. When `@SpringBootTest` searches for the application's configuration, it walks up the package hierarchy looking for exactly one `@SpringBootConfiguration` — if you have two, the test fails with an ambiguous configuration error.

**`@EnableAutoConfiguration`** is the trigger for Boot's auto-configuration pipeline. You can selectively disable auto-configurations using the `exclude` attribute: `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` removes database auto-configuration entirely. This is cleaner than adding dummy beans to satisfy conditions.

**`@ComponentScan`** is the one you'll customize most. When your package structure doesn't fit the "main class at the root" convention, use `scanBasePackages` to explicitly declare which packages to scan. The `scanBasePackageClasses` variant accepts a class reference instead of a string — this survives refactoring because the compiler catches renamed packages.

A typical override looks like `@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"com.example.core", "com.example.web"})`. This is safer than moving your main class to the root package, especially in multi-module projects where the root package might be too broad and accidentally scan transitive dependencies.

sections.title: When to Override Scan Defaults — Multi-Module Projects and the Test Discovery Rule
sections.content:
**In single-module projects**, the convention is simple: place the main class in the root package (`com.example.app`) and let `@ComponentScan` discover everything beneath it. This is the path of least resistance, and any deviation requires explicit configuration.

**In multi-module projects**, the root-package assumption breaks quickly. A common setup has a `core` module (`com.example.core`) and a `web` module (`com.example.web`) where the web module depends on core. If the main class lives in `com.example.web`, beans from `com.example.core` are in a sibling package — they will not be scanned. The fix is either `scanBasePackages = {"com.example"}` (scanning the shared parent) or `@Import(CoreConfiguration.class)` in the main class. The `@Import` approach is more surgical: you explicitly declare which configurations you depend on rather than accidentally scanning every class in the parent package.

**The test discovery rule** trips up teams regularly. When you run `@SpringBootTest`, Spring walks up the package tree from the test class to find the nearest `@SpringBootConfiguration`. If the test is in `com.example.web.controller` and the main class is in `com.example.web`, it's found correctly. But if you've placed the main class in a different package hierarchy, `@SpringBootTest` fails with `Unable to find a @SpringBootConfiguration`. The safest rule: keep test classes in a package that is the same as or a sub-package of the application's root package, or use `@SpringBootTest(classes = Application.class)` to point directly at the configuration class — bypassing the auto-discovery entirely.

Finally, the `scanBasePackageClasses` attribute is strictly better than `scanBasePackages` for refactoring safety. Instead of `scanBasePackages = {"com.example.core"}`, write `scanBasePackageClasses = {CoreMarker.class}` where `CoreMarker` is a placeholder interface in the `com.example.core` package. When the package is renamed, the compiler catches the reference — a string-based package name silently becomes wrong after a rename with no startup error.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootApplication` = `@Configuration` + `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan`** — decompose it when you only need part of the behavior.
- **Main class package determines the default scan boundary** — classes in `com.example.common` are invisible if the main class is in `com.example.app`; move the main class to the root package or use `scanBasePackages`.
- **`scanBasePackageClasses` is refactoring-safe; `scanBasePackages` (strings) is not** — renaming a package breaks the string reference silently; referencing a marker class fails at compile time.
- **`exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class}` prevents unwanted auto-config** — cleaner than `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` property because it is type-safe and visible at the annotation site.
- **Do not place `@SpringBootApplication` inside a sub-package** — the scan covers the annotated class's package and all sub-packages; a main class in `com.example.app.main` will not scan `com.example.app.service` if it is a sibling, not a descendant.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@SpringBootApplication` is a single annotation that composes three: `@Configuration` (this class is a bean source), `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (activate Spring Boot's auto-configuration), and `@ComponentScan` (scan from this class's package downward).

**The scan boundary rule**
- The component scan starts from the package containing the `@SpringBootApplication` class
- Place the main class in the root package (`com.example`) so every sub-package (`com.example.service`, `com.example.repository`) is automatically discovered
- A main class buried inside a sub-package means sibling packages are outside the scan boundary — beans there are invisible

**Customizing the scan**
- `@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = "com.example")` extends the boundary, but string-based — renaming the package breaks it silently
- `scanBasePackageClasses = {ServiceMarker.class}` is refactoring-safe — a compile error tells you immediately when the marker class moves

**Excluding auto-configurations**
- `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class})` prevents that auto-config from running — useful when a starter pulls in database config you do not want
- Type-safe and visible at the annotation site; prefer this over the string-based property approach

questions.question: How do application.properties, application.yml, and environment variables differ in Spring Boot configuration?
questions.title: application.properties vs application.yml vs Environment Variables
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot loads configuration from many sources and merges them into a unified Environment with a strict precedence order: OS environment variables and command-line arguments override application.yml, which overrides application.properties, which overrides default values. application.yml supports hierarchical structure and multi-document files, while application.properties is flat key=value pairs. Environment variables are essential for twelve-factor app deployments and are automatically mapped to property keys.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows precedence rules and can decide which mechanism to use in a given environment (local dev vs CI vs production Kubernetes).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming application.yml always wins over application.properties — in fact they have the same precedence, and if both exist Spring Boot loads both but yml is processed after properties, so yml values win for duplicates.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention profile-specific files (application-prod.yml), Spring Cloud Config Server, and the full 17-level PropertySource order documented in Spring Boot reference docs.

sections.title: The 17-Level Precedence Stack That Most Developers Get Wrong
sections.content:
The most common misconception is that `application.yml` overrides `application.properties` (or vice versa). **They have identical precedence** — if both exist with the same property, the one loaded last wins, and that depends on which Spring Boot version you're running. This is a trick question in interviews, and most candidates get it wrong.

What actually matters is Spring Boot's **17-level property source ordering.** Command-line arguments override environment variables, which override `application-{profile}.properties`, which override `application.properties`, which override `@PropertySource` annotations, which override defaults. The hierarchy goes from most specific (command line) to least specific (code defaults), and the first value found wins — Spring doesn't merge across levels.

This design solves a real deployment problem: you write defaults in `application.yml`, override per environment with `application-prod.yml`, override individual values at deploy time with environment variables (which play well with Docker and Kubernetes), and force values during debugging with command-line arguments. Each layer exists for a reason, and understanding the order prevents the most common production configuration bug — a value that works locally but gets silently overridden in deployment.

sections.title: Properties vs YAML vs Environment Variables — Format, Strength, and When Each Wins
sections.content:
The choice between formats isn't just syntax preference — each has genuine trade-offs that affect readability, tooling, and deployment.

| Aspect | application.properties | application.yml | Environment Variables |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Syntax** | Flat key=value pairs | Hierarchical YAML with indentation | `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` (uppercase, underscores) |
| **Precedence** | Same level as .yml | Same level as .properties | Higher — overrides both file types |
| **Multi-document** | Not supported | `---` separates profile sections in one file | N/A |
| **Type safety** | Strings only, no native lists | Lists, maps, nested objects natively | Strings only |
| **Tooling** | IDE autocomplete works well | Indentation errors cause silent failures | Platform-dependent (Docker, K8s) |
| **Secrets** | Visible in source control | Visible in source control | Injected at runtime, not in code |
| **Profile-specific** | `application-prod.properties` | `application-prod.yml` or multi-document | `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` |

**The practical recommendation:** use YAML for readable, hierarchical config in source control. Use environment variables for anything that changes per deployment — database URLs, API keys, feature flags. Never commit secrets in either file format. The combination of YAML defaults plus environment variable overrides is the pattern most production teams settle on.

sections.title: Profile-Specific Files and the External Config Pattern for Production
sections.content:
Spring Boot loads profile-specific files automatically: if `spring.profiles.active=prod`, then `application-prod.yml` is loaded and its properties override `application.yml`. This is the standard pattern for environment-specific configuration — database URLs, connection pool sizes, logging levels — without touching the base config.

**The external config directory pattern** takes this further. Spring Boot looks for config files in a `config/` subdirectory relative to the JAR's location before checking inside the JAR itself. In production, you can place an `application-prod.yml` in `config/` next to your JAR without rebuilding. This is how ops teams override individual values without developer involvement.

For complex deployments, **Spring Cloud Config Server** centralizes configuration across all services — it serves property values over HTTP, supports versioning through Git, and pushes changes without restarts using `@RefreshScope`. The full precedence from lowest to highest becomes: defaults in code → `application.yml` inside JAR → `application-{profile}.yml` inside JAR → external `config/` directory → Config Server → environment variables → command-line arguments.

One common pitfall: YAML indentation errors don't always cause startup failures. A misindented property silently becomes part of the wrong key, and you get the default value instead of your configured one. Always validate with `--debug` or the `/actuator/env` endpoint to confirm which values Spring actually loaded.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Properties and YAML at the same level have equal priority** — if both `application.properties` and `application.yml` exist in the same location, properties file wins for any key present in both; they are not merged cleanly.
- **Environment variables beat `application.properties` at every level** — Spring Boot's external configuration priority: command-line args > env vars > profile-specific properties > `application.properties`.
- **YAML null vs empty string** — `key:` (null) and `key: ""` (empty string) behave differently; `@Value("${key}")` on a null YAML property throws `IllegalArgumentException`.
- **Relaxed binding for env vars** — `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`; underscores replace dots and dashes; Spring Boot handles this automatically.
- **`spring.config.import` for external files** — import additional config from file system, classpath, or config servers: `spring.config.import=file:/etc/app/secrets.properties`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot aggregates configuration from multiple sources with a strict priority order. Knowing the order is essential for understanding why a property has a particular value in a given environment.

**Priority order (highest to lowest)**
- Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`) — always win
- Environment variables (`SERVER_PORT=9090`) — override property files; the standard for Docker and Kubernetes
- Profile-specific files (`application-prod.properties`) — override the base file for active profiles
- `application.properties` / `application.yml` — the base defaults

**Properties vs YAML**
- `application.properties`: flat key-value, readable, no indentation sensitivity
- `application.yml`: hierarchical structure, good for deeply nested config; but YAML null vs empty string behavior is a common trap — `key:` is null, which causes `@Value("${key}")` to throw `IllegalArgumentException`
- If both files exist at the same location, properties takes precedence for any key in both

**Environment variable relaxed binding**
- `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` automatically maps to `spring.datasource.url` — dots and dashes become underscores; uppercase is standard for container environments

Use property files for developer defaults, profile-specific files for environment overrides, and environment variables or secrets managers for production credentials — never hardcode credentials in any property file committed to version control.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator and how do you secure its endpoints in production?
questions.title: Spring Boot Actuator — Endpoints and Security
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot Actuator exposes operational HTTP (and JMX) endpoints for health checks, metrics, info, environment, thread dumps, and more. By default only /health and /info are exposed over HTTP; all others must be explicitly enabled. In production you should restrict actuator endpoints to an internal management port or secure them with Spring Security role-based access control to prevent information disclosure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that Actuator endpoints are a security risk if left open and can describe a layered defence strategy.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=* in production without any authentication, leaking environment variables, heap dumps, and internal metrics.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe using a separate management.server.port with a firewall rule so only internal services reach Actuator, plus /actuator/health groups for liveness and readiness probes in Kubernetes.

sections.title: Actuator Is Production Observability Out of the Box — And a Security Liability If Left Open
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready endpoints to your application — `/health`, `/metrics`, `/env`, `/beans`, `/heapdump`, `/threaddump`, and more. These endpoints give you instant visibility into your running application without writing any custom monitoring code. The problem is that several of these endpoints expose **dangerously sensitive information.**

`/env` shows every environment variable — including database passwords and API keys if they're injected that way. `/heapdump` lets anyone download a full heap snapshot containing in-memory secrets, session tokens, and decrypted credentials. `/beans` reveals your entire application architecture. Setting `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production — which many tutorials recommend for development — is the most common Actuator security mistake.

**The default in Spring Boot 2.x+ is conservative by design:** only `/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP. Everything else requires explicit opt-in. But the real production strategy isn't just about which endpoints to expose — it's a layered defense combining endpoint selection, authentication, network isolation, and health check design.

sections.title: Controlling Exposure — Which Endpoints to Enable and How to Lock Down the Rest
Network Isolation — The Separate Management Port That Changes Everything
sections.content:
The strongest security measure isn't authentication — it's **network isolation.** Setting `management.server.port=9090` moves all Actuator endpoints to a separate port. In Kubernetes or any cloud deployment, you expose port 8080 to the internet through the ingress but keep port 9090 accessible only from the internal network.

This means `/heapdump`, `/env`, and `/threaddump` are never reachable from the public internet regardless of authentication configuration. Even if someone discovers a vulnerability in your security setup, the management port isn't routed through the load balancer. Combine this with `management.server.address=127.0.0.1` in single-server deployments to bind management endpoints exclusively to localhost.

The management port also supports its own SSL configuration via `management.server.ssl.*` properties, so you can require mutual TLS for internal services accessing Actuator while serving the main app over standard HTTPS.

sections.title: Health Groups — Separate Liveness and Readiness Probes for Kubernetes
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.3+ introduced **health groups** that solve a specific Kubernetes problem: liveness and readiness probes need different health indicators. A liveness probe should check "is this process alive and not deadlocked" — if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod. A readiness probe should check "can this pod serve traffic" — if it fails, the pod is removed from the service's endpoints.

Including a database health check in the liveness probe is a common mistake. If the database goes down, every pod gets restarted — which is worse than useless because the database is still down and now you've triggered a cascading restart. The database check belongs in the readiness probe, where a failure means "stop sending traffic to this pod" but doesn't trigger a restart.

Spring Boot exposes `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` automatically when running in a Kubernetes environment (detected via the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` environment variable). You configure which indicators belong to each group in properties. The readiness group typically includes database, Redis, and message broker checks, while liveness stays minimal — usually just the default ping.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never expose `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production** — `/actuator/env` dumps all properties including passwords and tokens; `/actuator/heapdump` gives attackers the full JVM heap.
- **Separate management port isolates actuator from the application** — `management.server.port=9090` with a firewall rule that blocks port 9090 from public internet is the production-safe pattern.
- **`/actuator/health` vs `/actuator/health/**` have different content** — the root endpoint shows `UP`/`DOWN`; the detail endpoints (`/actuator/health/db`, `/actuator/health/diskSpace`) show component-level information that may leak connection strings.
- **Custom `HealthIndicator` beans integrate external checks** — implement `HealthIndicator`, return `Health.up()` or `Health.down().withDetail("reason", msg)`; Spring Boot includes it in `/health` automatically.
- **`/actuator/metrics` and `/actuator/prometheus` expose performance data** — integrate with Prometheus/Grafana by adding `micrometer-registry-prometheus`; no code changes required beyond the dependency.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator gives you production visibility — health checks, metrics, environment inspection, thread dumps — without deploying a separate monitoring agent. The default configuration is safe for development. Exposing it fully in production is a security incident waiting to happen.

**Security hardening**
- By default only `/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP
- `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` exposes everything — including `/env` (dumps all properties with passwords), `/heapdump` (full JVM memory), `/shutdown` (remote shutdown)
- Expose only what monitoring infrastructure needs: `include=health,info,metrics,prometheus`

**Isolating the management port**
- `management.server.port=9090` moves all actuator endpoints to a separate port
- A firewall or network policy allows only internal monitoring systems to reach port 9090; port 8080 remains public-facing
- This is the standard pattern for production: no authentication overhead on the main port, no public exposure on the management port

**Health endpoint detail**
- `/actuator/health` returns only `UP` or `DOWN` by default — safe to expose publicly for load balancer checks
- `management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized` reveals database connection status and disk space only to authenticated users

Custom `HealthIndicator` beans are how you add application-specific checks — external API reachability, queue depth thresholds, license expiry — integrated into the same `/health` response that your monitoring system already watches.

questions.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value
questions.direct_answer: @Value injects a single property value using SpEL and is convenient for one-off values, but it does not support validation, relaxed binding, or IDE autocompletion. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole prefix of related properties to a typed POJO, supports JSR-303 Bean Validation, relaxed binding, and generates IDE metadata — making it the preferred choice whenever you have more than one or two related properties.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the practical limitations of @Value and can justify when the more verbose @ConfigurationProperties approach is worth it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Value for every property, even large groups of related config, resulting in classes littered with @Value fields and no validation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @ConfigurationProperties requires @EnableConfigurationProperties or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan, supports constructor binding (immutable records in Java 16+), and that spring-boot-configuration-processor generates additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json for IDE hints.

sections.title: Why @Value Breaks Down at Scale and @ConfigurationProperties Exists to Fix It
sections.content:
In small applications with three or four properties, `@Value("${some.prop}")` works fine. The problem appears when you have **20+ related configuration values** — database pool settings, retry policies, feature flags — scattered across multiple beans. Each `@Value` field is a raw string injection with no type safety, no validation, and no IDE support for refactoring. Rename a property key in `application.yml` and nothing fails at compile time — you get a runtime `IllegalArgumentException` or worse, a silent null.

`@ConfigurationProperties` solves this by **binding an entire prefix of your configuration to a typed Java object.** Instead of twenty `@Value` annotations, you get a single POJO with fields that match the property keys. Spring Boot's relaxed binding handles `camelCase`, `kebab-case`, and `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` automatically. You get IDE autocomplete for your custom properties through `spring-boot-configuration-processor`, JSR-303 validation with `@Validated`, and immutable configuration using constructor binding.

The trade-off is setup overhead. `@ConfigurationProperties` requires either `@EnableConfigurationProperties(MyProps.class)` on a configuration class or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` on the main class. For a single property, that's unnecessary ceremony. The dividing line is clear: **one or two isolated properties → `@Value`; a group of related properties → `@ConfigurationProperties`.**

sections.title: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties — What Each Actually Gives You
sections.content:
The differences go beyond syntax — they affect testability, safety, and how configuration evolves as the application grows.

| Aspect | @Value | @ConfigurationProperties |
|---|---|---|
| **Binding** | Single property per annotation | Entire prefix mapped to a POJO |
| **Type safety** | String by default, manual conversion | Automatic type conversion + nested objects |
| **Validation** | No built-in validation | `@Validated` with JSR-303 annotations (`@NotNull`, `@Min`) |
| **IDE support** | No autocomplete for custom props | `spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates metadata |
| **Immutability** | Mutable fields only | Constructor binding with `@ConstructorBinding` (pre-3.x) or record classes |
| **SpEL support** | Full SpEL: `#{T(Math).random()}` | No SpEL — pure property binding |
| **Refactoring** | Rename breaks silently at runtime | Type-safe, caught at startup |
| **Testing** | Inject via `@TestPropertySource` | Instantiate POJO directly in unit tests |

**The SpEL point is the exception where `@Value` wins.** If you need a computed default like `@Value("#{${retry.max:3} * 2}")`, `@ConfigurationProperties` can't do that. But SpEL in configuration is a code smell in most cases — prefer computing values in code.

sections.title: Constructor Binding and Why Java Records Make @ConfigurationProperties Even Better
sections.content:
In Spring Boot 3.x, `@ConfigurationProperties` classes can be Java `record` types — immutable by default with no boilerplate. A record like `record DatabaseProps(String url, int maxPoolSize, Duration connectionTimeout) {}` bound to the `app.database` prefix gives you type-safe, immutable, validated configuration with zero getters or setters.

**The `spring-boot-configuration-processor` annotation processor** generates `META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json` at compile time. This file powers IDE autocomplete — when you type `app.database.` in `application.yml`, your IDE suggests `url`, `max-pool-size`, and `connection-timeout` with their types and descriptions. Without the processor, your custom properties show warnings in the IDE as "unknown property."

For testability, `@ConfigurationProperties` POJOs can be instantiated directly without Spring context — `new DatabaseProps("jdbc:h2:mem:test", 5, Duration.ofSeconds(3))` in a unit test. With `@Value`, you need `@SpringBootTest` or `@TestPropertySource` to inject values, which means slower tests and unnecessary context loading.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` requires `@EnableConfigurationProperties` or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`** — or the class must be annotated with `@Component`; without one of these, the POJO is never populated.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` validates at startup; `@Value` validates at first use** — `@Validated` + JSR-303 annotations on a `@ConfigurationProperties` class fail startup with a clear message listing every missing required field.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` auto-converts `Duration`, `DataSize`, and `List`** — `timeout: 30s` binds to a `Duration` field automatically; `@Value` requires manual parsing.
- **`@Value` for one-off values; `@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix** — three related properties sharing a prefix = migrate to `@ConfigurationProperties`.
- **Spring Boot's annotation processor generates IDE metadata** — add `spring-boot-configuration-processor` as an annotation processor; your custom properties get auto-completion and documentation in IDEs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties` both inject external configuration, but they are designed for different scales. Choosing the wrong one creates code that is hard to test, hard to validate, and hard for teammates to discover.

**`@Value` — for isolated one-off values**
- `@Value("${api.key}")` injects a single property; works fine for one or two standalone values
- No validation at startup — a missing required property causes an NPE at the first call site, not at startup
- No type conversion for structured types — `Duration`, `DataSize`, `List` require manual parsing

**`@ConfigurationProperties` — for groups of related properties**
- Binds an entire prefix to a POJO: `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment")` maps `payment.url`, `payment.timeout`, `payment.retries` to fields automatically
- Add `@Validated` and JSR-303 annotations — missing required fields cause a clear startup failure with every violation listed
- Auto-converts `Duration` (`30s`), `DataSize` (`256MB`), `List` (comma-separated strings)
- Generates IDE auto-completion metadata when `spring-boot-configuration-processor` is added as an annotation processor

**Activation**
- The class needs either `@Component`, `@EnableConfigurationProperties(MyConfig.class)` in a `@Configuration` class, or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` on the main class

The rule: `@Value` for a single isolated key, `@ConfigurationProperties` for anything that has a prefix and more than two properties.

questions.question: How do you configure and implement graceful shutdown in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Graceful Shutdown in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Since Spring Boot 2.3, graceful shutdown is built in: set server.shutdown=graceful and optionally spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase to control how long the application waits for in-flight requests to complete before forcing shutdown. When a SIGTERM is received, the embedded server stops accepting new requests while existing requests drain, then the Spring context closes in reverse bean-creation order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows graceful shutdown is a first-class feature since 2.3 and understands the drain-then-close sequence, not just adding a shutdown hook manually.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Implementing a custom ShutdownHook via Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook() and missing the coordinated context close that Spring already provides.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Kubernetes SIGTERM plus terminationGracePeriodSeconds must be coordinated with spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, and mention SmartLifecycle for custom beans that need ordered shutdown.

sections.title: Why Runtime.addShutdownHook Is Wrong and Spring's Coordinated Shutdown Exists
sections.content:
The most common mistake is implementing graceful shutdown with `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook()` and trying to manually drain connections. This bypasses Spring's coordinated shutdown lifecycle entirely — your hook races against Spring's own context close, and you end up with beans destroyed while requests are still in flight. Database connections get closed while active transactions are running; message producer sessions get torn down before queued messages flush. The result is partial writes, lost acknowledgments, and clients receiving connection-reset errors instead of clean responses.

**Spring Boot 2.3+ provides built-in graceful shutdown** with a single property: `server.shutdown=graceful`. When this is set, the embedded server stops accepting new requests on SIGTERM but continues processing in-flight requests until they complete or a timeout expires. The timeout is controlled by `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`, which defaults to 30 seconds. This property applies per-phase — the drain phase and the context-close phase each get this budget independently.

This matters because modern deployments run in containers orchestrated by Kubernetes, ECS, or Docker Compose. When Kubernetes decides to terminate a pod, it sends SIGTERM and waits for `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30 seconds) before force-killing with SIGKILL. **Your Spring shutdown timeout must be shorter than the Kubernetes grace period** — otherwise Kubernetes kills the process before Spring finishes draining, and in-flight requests get hard-terminated. The correct pattern is to set `timeout-per-shutdown-phase` to at least 5 seconds less than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, leaving a buffer for OS-level process teardown between Spring completing its shutdown and Kubernetes giving up.

sections.title: How Spring's Shutdown Sequence Actually Works When SIGTERM Arrives
sections.content:
When SIGTERM is received, Spring's shutdown follows a specific, deterministic order. **First, the embedded web server stops accepting new connections** — the server socket closes, any new TCP connections are refused, and the health check endpoint begins returning DOWN for readiness. Load balancers detecting this almost immediately stop routing new requests here.

Second, in-flight requests continue processing. Each request runs to completion or until the `timeout-per-shutdown-phase` budget expires. If a request hasn't finished by the timeout, Spring interrupts the thread — this is why long-running operations need cooperative cancellation logic. An `@Async` task that doesn't check thread interruption status will run past the timeout and get forcefully terminated by SIGKILL.

Third, Spring publishes `ContextClosedEvent` and begins destroying beans in reverse creation order. `@PreDestroy` methods run here — closing database connection pools, flushing message queue producers, unregistering from service discovery registries. **This phase happens after complete request draining**, which is why `@PreDestroy` is safe for resource cleanup: no requests are active when connections are returned to pools.

```yaml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
```

For beans that need fine-grained control over teardown order — for example, a message consumer that must stop consuming before the database connection pool closes — implement `SmartLifecycle`. Return a `phase` value from `getPhase()`: lower phase numbers stop first. `@PreDestroy` is sufficient for most cases, but `SmartLifecycle` gives you ordering guarantees that `@PreDestroy` cannot provide.

sections.title: The Kubernetes Timing Trap — When Your Grace Period Is Shorter Than Your Shutdown
sections.content:
The most dangerous misconfiguration is setting `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=60s` while Kubernetes has `terminationGracePeriodSeconds=30`. After 30 seconds, Kubernetes sends SIGKILL — your application is forcefully terminated mid-drain. Clients see connection resets, in-flight database transactions are rolled back, and message acknowledgments are never sent. This failure mode is invisible during local development because developers rarely test shutdown under realistic load with Kubernetes timing.

**The readiness probe interval compounds the problem.** When SIGTERM arrives, Spring immediately marks the readiness probe as DOWN so Kubernetes stops routing new requests to the pod. But if your readiness probe `periodSeconds` is set to 30 (a common default), the load balancer won't discover the pod is unhealthy for up to 30 more seconds — during which it's still sending new requests while the application is trying to drain. Reduce `periodSeconds` to 5–10 seconds in production for fast de-registration.

For **WebSocket connections and Server-Sent Events**, Spring's built-in graceful shutdown handles HTTP request/response cycles only. Long-lived connections need explicit handling. Register an `ApplicationListener<ContextClosedEvent>` that iterates open WebSocket sessions and sends a proper close frame (`CloseStatus.GOING_AWAY`) before the connection infrastructure is torn down. Without this, clients receive an abrupt TCP disconnect instead of a clean WebSocket close handshake, triggering aggressive reconnect logic that may overwhelm the remaining healthy instances.

A final production checklist: verify that `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` is shorter than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` by at least 5 seconds, readiness probe `periodSeconds` is 5–10 seconds, and any `@Async` tasks can be interrupted cleanly within the timeout window.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`server.shutdown=graceful` + `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s`** — enables graceful shutdown; Spring Boot waits up to the configured timeout for in-flight requests to complete before closing.
- **Do not register `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook()` manually** — Spring Boot already registers a JVM shutdown hook; adding another creates unpredictable ordering between your hook and Spring's context close.
- **Kubernetes SIGTERM + `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` must align** — Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30s) before SIGKILL; your `timeout-per-shutdown-phase` must be shorter than that value or pods are killed mid-drain.
- **`@PreDestroy` runs during shutdown — after in-flight requests drain** — safe for releasing connection pools and deregistering from service registries.
- **Actuator `/actuator/shutdown` must be explicitly enabled and secured** — `management.endpoint.shutdown.enabled=true`; never expose without authentication — it remotely terminates the application.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Graceful shutdown means the application stops accepting new requests and waits for in-flight ones to complete before closing — rather than killing active connections immediately on SIGTERM.

**Enabling it**
- `server.shutdown=graceful` — Spring Boot's web server stops accepting new connections but lets active requests finish
- `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s` — the maximum wait time; requests still active after this threshold are terminated

**The Kubernetes integration pattern**
- Kubernetes sends SIGTERM when a pod is removed; waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` before sending SIGKILL
- Your `timeout-per-shutdown-phase` must be shorter than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` — if Spring is still draining when Kubernetes sends SIGKILL, active requests are killed anyway
- Typical setup: `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60`, `timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 50s` — Spring gets 50 seconds to drain, Kubernetes terminates at 60

**What not to do**
- Do not add `Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook()` manually — Spring Boot already registers a shutdown hook that closes the `ApplicationContext`; a second hook creates race conditions between the two

`@PreDestroy` methods on singleton beans execute during the Spring context close phase, which happens after the web server stops accepting requests. This is the correct place to release database connections, close Kafka producers, and deregister from service discovery.

questions.question: How do you write and register a custom Spring Boot auto-configuration?
questions.title: Custom Auto-Configuration (spring.factories / AutoConfiguration.imports)
questions.direct_answer: Create a @AutoConfiguration class with @ConditionalOn* guards, implement your @Bean methods, then register the class in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (Spring Boot 2.7+) so Spring Boot discovers it at startup. This pattern is used by every Spring Boot starter to provide zero-configuration library integration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the registration mechanism and knows how to write safe conditions so the auto-configuration backs off correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to add the registration file, so the @AutoConfiguration class is never discovered, or using @Configuration instead of @AutoConfiguration which bypasses ordering guarantees.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the full starter module layout (autoconfigure JAR + starter POM), explain how @AutoConfigureAfter/@AutoConfigureBefore work, and show how spring-boot-configuration-processor generates IDE metadata from @ConfigurationProperties.

sections.title: The Registration File Most Developers Forget — And Why Their Auto-Configuration Silently Does Nothing
sections.content:
The number one mistake when writing custom auto-configuration is forgetting the registration file. You create a perfectly valid `@AutoConfiguration` class with all the right conditions, but Spring Boot never discovers it because **auto-configuration classes are not found by component scanning.** They must be explicitly listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` (Boot 2.7+) or `META-INF/spring.factories` (pre-2.7).

This is intentional. Auto-configuration classes live in shared libraries — JARs consumed by other applications. Component scanning would only find them if the consumer happened to scan the right package, making the behavior dependent on the consumer's package structure. The registration file makes discovery explicit and package-independent.

The standard pattern for production library auto-configuration is a **two-module layout**: an `autoconfigure` module containing the `@AutoConfiguration` class, its `@ConfigurationProperties` POJO, and the registration file; and a `starter` module that depends on the autoconfigure module plus all required transitive dependencies. **The starter POM has no Java code** — it's a dependency aggregator. Consumers add a single `<dependency>` to their POM, and the transitive dependency brings in the autoconfigure module where the actual logic lives.

This separation matters because it lets consumers who need fine-grained control depend only on the `autoconfigure` module directly, bypassing the starter's default transitive dependencies. Spring's own starters follow this exact pattern — `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` is just a POM that pulls in `spring-boot-autoconfigure` (among others). Understanding this structure is what interviewers test when they ask you to design a reusable library: you should immediately reach for this two-module layout rather than bundling configuration inside the same module as the library API.

Key Points

- **Starter layout: two modules** — `my-feature-autoconfigure` (contains `@AutoConfiguration` + `@Conditional` logic); `my-feature-spring-boot-starter` (POM-only, depends on autoconfigure + feature library).
- **User beans always win — put `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on every auto-configured bean** — this lets users override any default by defining their own bean of that type.
- **`@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` controls ordering** — if your auto-config depends on a `DataSource` bean existing first, declare the dependency explicitly.
- **Test auto-configuration with `ApplicationContextRunner`** — creates a minimal application context without starting Spring Boot; call `.withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(YourAutoConfig.class))` and assert which beans are registered.

- Use `@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` when your beans depend on a `DataSource` being available

**Testing**
- `ApplicationContextRunner` is the standard testing tool — creates a minimal context, applies your auto-configuration, and lets you assert which beans registered
- No need to start the full application; tests run in milliseconds
